pages.title: Getting started
pages.summary: What the FireHouse part of WordPress holds, who can change what, and where to find help.
pages.html:
What the FireHouse part of WordPress holds, who can change what, and where to find help.

What you look after

The FireHouse is a section of the site at /firehouse/. In WordPress you look after four things:

  • Projects: one for each research project a researcher submitted through the survey. You review each one, add a few words of your own, and decide when it's published.
  • Topic areas: the four areas the needs are grouped into, such as Warnings and Immediate Response. You keep their short names and descriptions up to date.
  • The synthesis: the top needs in each topic area, across all the published projects. You make it in NotebookLM, or have a model draft it with Analyze results, then check it and publish it.
  • The landing and About pages: their headings, text and buttons, and the About page's team.

The FireHouse menu

Everything is under FireHouse in the menu on the left of the dashboard.

  • Projects lists every project. Choose a title to open it.
  • Topics lists the four topic areas.
  • Settings holds the site name, the Submit a Finding button, the navigation labels, the switch that opens the survey form, the survey form's questions and, on a site with a Workers AI key, the prompt Analyze results sends.
  • Import loads content from the survey's records. Only administrators see it.
  • Synthesis is where you publish a reviewed synthesis, and, on a site with a Workers AI key, have a model draft one.
  • Help, at the end, is this guide.

The landing and About pages are under Pages, as "The FireHouse" and the About page under it. While the survey form is open, its Submit page is under "The FireHouse" too.

What a FireHouse Editor can and can't do

The FireHouse Editor role can change the FireHouse and nothing else on the site:

  • You can edit and publish projects, edit the topic areas, change the words on the landing and About pages, change the FireHouse settings, and publish a synthesis.
  • You can't change the site's other pages or posts, add or remove pages, or upload images. An administrator does those.
  • You can't change what a researcher wrote. Their answers are shown exactly as they submitted them.

Getting help

On each FireHouse screen, choose Help at the top right of the screen. It opens the part of this guide for that screen. FireHouse → Help has the whole guide, with screenshots. The editor for the landing and About pages has no Help tab: see Changing the landing and About pages.

This guide comes with the plugin, so it matches the version installed on this site.

pages.title: Reviewing and publishing a project
pages.summary: How to review a project, add the FireHouse team's words, publish it, and take it off the site.
pages.html:
How to review a project, add the FireHouse team's words, publish it, and take it off the site.

Where projects come from

Each project is one researcher's answers to the survey. An administrator brings new answers into WordPress on FireHouse → Import. A new project arrives with everything the researcher wrote, as a draft for you to review, unless the team decided before the import to publish it.

If an administrator has turned on the FireHouse survey form (FireHouse → Settings), each submission also arrives as a draft, and the team mailbox gets an email with a link to it. The email holds nothing the researcher wrote: open the draft to read it.

Soon after a submission arrives, while it's still a draft, each publication the researcher gave by DOI gets its title, journal and year under Publications, looked up as the import looks them up. One that couldn't be looked up shows only its DOI or address.

Open a project

  1. Go to FireHouse → Projects.
  2. Choose the project's title. Drafts show "Draft" after their title; a project that can't be published shows "No IRB approval".

What you can change

A project's screen has two boxes.

Editorial fields are the FireHouse team's own words. You can change them at any time:

  • Summary: one or two lines under the title on the project explorer's tiles. The import starts it with the abstract's first sentence; shorten or rewrite it.
  • Publication status: whether the research has been published, shown at the top of the project's page. The survey doesn't ask, so it starts as None.
  • Geography note: a few words beside the project's regions on its page, such as "Front Range". Leave it empty if the survey names no region.
  • Full record link: where the full record is kept, starting with https:// or http://. The project's page links to it as "View full record".

From the survey shows the researcher's answers, exactly as they submitted them. You can't change them here. If an answer needs correcting, tell the developer: the correction goes into the survey's records, you confirm it, and the next import brings it in. A survey form submission has no such record: see Reviewing a survey form submission.

A project sent through the FireHouse survey form also has a Private answers box on the right: the submitter's email, their job title, and how they shared their results. Only the FireHouse team and the site's administrators see it. It never appears on the site, and you can't change it.

When you've made your changes, choose Update (or Save Draft for a draft) in the Publish box.

Publish a project

  1. Read the researcher's answers and fill in the editorial fields.
  2. Choose Save Draft.
  3. Choose Preview to see the project's page as visitors will. Preview shows the project as last saved, which is why you save first.
  4. Choose Publish.

The project then appears in the project explorer and in the landing page's counts, and on the topic pages once a synthesis names it.

A project can be published only if the researcher recorded IRB approval or an exemption in the survey. If they didn't, the Publish box says "This project can't be published", the Projects list marks it "No IRB approval", and you can still save it as a draft. Approval comes from the survey's records, not this screen.

Once a project has been published, its address (its link) can't change, because people may have shared it. That's true even if it goes back to being a draft.

Take a project off the site

  • To hide it for now: in the Publish box, next to Status, choose Edit, choose Draft, then OK and Update. It leaves the site, and you can publish it again later.
  • To remove it: choose Move to Trash. It leaves the site. To bring it back, open Trash in FireHouse → Projects and choose Restore under its title. It comes back as a draft, so publish it again.
  • To delete it for good: in FireHouse → Projects, open Trash, and choose Delete Permanently under its title. That removes it with its fields and its revisions, and can't be undone.

Either way, it also leaves the needs that name it on the topic pages, and their project counts go down until the next synthesis.

Before you delete a project for good, tell an administrator. The next import brings back any project that's still in the survey's records, as a new project. And while a project is in the Trash, the import stops until it's restored or deleted.

Undo a change

Each save keeps a revision. In the Publish box, next to Revisions, choose Browse to compare versions. Move the slider to the version you want and choose Restore This Revision. That puts back the summary, the publication status and the full record link as they were, but not the geography note. It never changes the researcher's answers.

If something isn't saved

  • "Editorial fields not saved": a field has a problem, such as a full record link that isn't a web address. None of the editorial fields were saved, and each problem is marked. Your other changes, such as publishing it, were saved. Fix what's marked and save again.
  • "The screen had been open too long": the editorial fields weren't saved. They're still on the screen as you typed them: save again.
  • "This field has characters that can't be stored": retype the field rather than pasting it.

pages.title: Reviewing a survey form submission
pages.summary: What to do when a researcher sends the FireHouse survey form: find their submission, check it, then publish it or set it aside.
pages.html:
What to do when a researcher sends the FireHouse survey form: find their submission, check it, then publish it or set it aside.

When a submission arrives

While an administrator has the survey form turned on (FireHouse → Settings), each submission arrives as a draft project. Nothing a researcher sends appears on the site until one of you publishes it.

The team mailbox gets an email, "New FireHouse submission", with a link to the draft and a link to every draft. The email holds nothing the researcher wrote: open the draft to read it. If the researcher said the project has no IRB approval or exemption, the email's subject says so.

Find it

  • Choose the link in the email, or go to FireHouse → Projects and choose Draft at the top of the list.
  • At the bottom of the From the survey box, a submission's Response ID starts with W_. A project brought in on the Import screen has another kind of ID.

Check it

From the survey shows the researcher's answers exactly as they sent them. Check that the project meets the form's inclusion criteria:

  • it's about end users and fire weather, in any phase of the fire cycle;
  • it's finished;
  • any research with people in it was approved by an IRB, or exempt;
  • it's one project, not a researcher's whole body of work.

Soon after a submission arrives, while it's still a draft, each publication the researcher gave by DOI gets its title, journal and year under Publications. One that couldn't be looked up shows only its DOI or address, and so does every publication in a submission without IRB approval.

If the researcher answered any of the private questions, the Private answers box on the right holds the submitter's email, their job title, and how they've shared their results. Only the FireHouse team and the site's administrators see it, and it never appears on the site. Use the email to follow up with the researcher. These questions are optional, so a submission may have no email.

Publish it

Fill in the editorial fields and publish it as you would any project: see Reviewing and publishing a project.

A submission without IRB approval or exemption can't be published. It stays a draft, marked "No IRB approval" in the Projects list.

Correct it

You can't change a researcher's answers. If one needs correcting:

  • If it has never been published: ask the researcher, if they gave an email, to send the form again with the correction. When the new draft arrives, delete the first one, as below.
  • If it has been published, even if it's a draft again now: don't delete it. Its address, your editorial fields and the synthesis's links to it would go with it, and a new submission doesn't bring them back. Tell the developer instead.

Set it aside or delete it

  • If it doesn't meet the criteria: leave it as a draft while the team decides, or delete it.
  • If it's junk or a test, or was sent twice: delete it, keeping the newer of two.

To delete a submission, choose Move to Trash, then open Trash in FireHouse → Projects and choose Delete Permanently under its title. Deleting it permanently also deletes its private answers, and so does WordPress emptying the Trash, which it does by itself, usually 30 days after something is put there. While the project is kept, its private answers are kept too, and you can't clear them. How long they may be kept waits on NOAA's privacy review.

The form turns away most automated submissions. If junk keeps getting through, tell an administrator.

To reword a question on the form, see FireHouse settings.

pages.title: Editing a topic area
pages.summary: How to change a topic area's short label, description and what it covers.
pages.html:
How to change a topic area's short label, description and what it covers.

The four topic areas

Every need is grouped into one of four topic areas: Observations and Monitoring; Forecasts and Modeling; Warnings and Immediate Response; and Strategic Adaptation and Institutional Governance. There are always these four: they can't be added or removed, and their addresses don't change. The Edit button beside the Permalink changes nothing.

Go to FireHouse → Topics and choose an area's title to open it.

What you can change

The Topic fields box holds the FireHouse team's words for the area:

  • Label (at the top): the area's full name, such as "Warnings and Immediate Response". It's the heading on the area's page.
  • Short label: a word or two, such as "Warnings", on the area's tags and in its page's breadcrumb. It's required.
  • Description: one sentence on what the area is about. It isn't shown on the site; the synthesis reads it as the area's description.
  • What this area covers: one item per line, such as "Surface observation networks". The area's page lists them beside its needs. Leave it empty to leave that box out.

Choose Update to save. The label is saved on its own, and can't be empty: an empty one is put back as it was. The Topic fields are saved together, all or none: if one has a problem, the screen says which, keeps what you typed, and saves none of them.

Preview Changes shows the label as you typed it, but the area's other words as they were last updated. Update the topic to see them.

The synthesis of needs

Below the topic fields, Synthesis of needs shows the area's top needs from the last synthesis, who reviewed it, and when. You can't change them here: a new synthesis replaces them, on FireHouse → Synthesis. See Publishing a synthesis.

Until someone has reviewed the synthesis, "Reviewed by" says "No one yet", and the area's page marks its needs "Draft, pending team review".

Undo a change

Each update keeps a revision. Choose Browse next to Revisions in the Publish box, move the slider to the version you want, and choose Restore This Revision. Restoring a revision also puts back the synthesis the area had then.

pages.title: Publishing a synthesis
pages.summary: How to make a new synthesis of the top needs, with Analyze results or in NotebookLM, check it, and publish it to the topic pages and the landing page.
pages.html:
How to make a new synthesis of the top needs, with Analyze results or in NotebookLM, check it, and publish it to the topic pages and the landing page.

What the synthesis is

The synthesis reads every published project together and lists up to five needs in each topic area, each with how many projects raise it and which ones. It's the one place the site puts researchers' findings in other words, so nothing reaches the site until someone on the FireHouse team has reviewed it.

Make a new one when projects have been published or taken off the site since the last.

There are two ways to make one. Either way, it goes through the same check and Mark reviewed step.

  • Analyze results, on FireHouse → Synthesis, has a model on Cloudflare Workers AI draft it. You see it only on a site an administrator has given a Workers AI key; see the next section.
  • NotebookLM: download the source, run the team's prompt in the notebook, and paste the result. Start at step 1.

Analyze results

The model is sent the published projects, word for word, the four topic areas, and the prompt on FireHouse → Settings. Nothing private goes, and no earlier synthesis.

  1. On FireHouse → Synthesis, under Analyze results, pick a Model and choose Analyze results.
  2. The model drafts in the background, which takes a few minutes. Reload the page to see when it's done. One model drafts at a time.
  3. Each model's latest draft is kept under its name, so you can have several draft and compare them. Its whole reply shows everything the model wrote, with the entries each need draws on if the model gave them: the prompt asks for them, but not every model gives them. The prompt it was given shows the prompt it ran.
  4. Choose Check under the draft you want: the button names the model, as in "Check Llama 4 Scout (Meta)'s draft". Its JSON goes into the box at the bottom and is checked, as in step 4 below, and Made with starts with the model's name.
  5. Review it as in step 3, with the model's whole reply, which stays under the needs while you check and edit, in place of NotebookLM's citations. Where the reply doesn't give the entries behind a need, read the projects the need names, on their pages, before you keep it. Then mark it reviewed as in step 5.

To compare models, have each draft with the same prompt, then check each in turn: the screen shows the needs each would publish. Checking one drops the check before it, so mark reviewed only the one the team chooses.

A draft that failed says why. Workers AI may have refused the request or be busy, or the reply may hold no JSON or have stopped at its length limit. Try again, or try another model. If one says it never started, tell an administrator: the site's scheduled tasks may not be running. If one says it didn't finish, try again, and tell an administrator if it happens again.

The reply is the model's, not the team's: read it as a draft. If it holds a character that doesn't show, the screen says so, since it may then read differently from what it says. If the site shows a different number of projects from the number the model read, checking the draft says so. It compares only the number, so it can't tell when one project was published and another taken off in between: after any change to which projects are published, have the model draft again before you mark it reviewed.

1. Download the source

Go to FireHouse → Synthesis and choose Download NotebookLM source. You get firehouse-findings.md: every published project, word for word, and the four topic areas.

2. Run the prompt in NotebookLM

  1. In the FireHouse notebook, delete the old firehouse-findings.md source and upload the one you downloaded. Keep it the notebook's only source, so the synthesis can't draw on anything the site doesn't show.
  2. In the notebook's chat, run the team's prompt. The current prompt is in the FireHouse repository's NotebookLM notes.

3. Review it

NotebookLM answers with the needs and their citations, then a block of JSON that starts with [ and ends with ]. Check each need against the projects it came from, with NotebookLM's citations, and edit the wording: the published words are the team's, not the model's.

Edit the JSON in the box on FireHouse → Synthesis, or in a plain-text editor such as Notepad. Don't use Word or Google Docs: they change the quotation marks, and the screen can't read it then. A need's words are its "text", its count is its "mentions" number, and its projects are its "projects" list.

  • In each area, put the needs in order of their project count, highest first. The prompt lists the most important need first, so you'll usually reorder them: the check refuses any other order. For a tie, put first the need that applies across more agencies or regions.
  • Each need's count must equal the number of projects it lists. If you take a project out of a need, lower its count.

Keep a copy of your edited version until it's published.

4. Check it

  1. Copy the block, from its first [ to its last ].
  2. Paste it into The JSON the prompt gave, and choose Check the synthesis.
  3. If the screen says "Not ready", it lists each problem. Fix them in the box and check again. Nothing is written until the check finds nothing wrong.

A model can shorten or reword a project's page slug, stop it partway, or make its own from the project's title. When a need names a project the site doesn't have, the check gives the page slug that name most likely means, with its project's title, when one clearly stands out. Change the name to it only if the need draws on that project. If that project isn't published, the check says so: take it out of the need.

5. Mark it reviewed

When the screen says "Ready to mark reviewed", read the needs it shows. Reviewed by starts with the name your account shows, and the topic pages show it to visitors: type the names as the team wants them published. Made with starts with NotebookLM, or with the model's name for a draft from Analyze results. Then choose Mark reviewed and publish.

The topic pages and the landing page show the new synthesis at once, with today's date.

Mark it reviewed within thirty minutes of the check. If you wait longer, or open FireHouse → Synthesis again in between, the check is dropped, and you check it again.

If it says "Not published: the projects changed since the check", a project was published or taken off the site in between. The screen has checked it again: review the needs, then mark it reviewed. If it says "Not published: this check isn't waiting any more", check it again.

Undo it

Each topic area keeps the synthesis it had before as a revision. To go back, open each of the four areas under FireHouse → Topics, choose Browse next to Revisions, move the slider one step to the left, and choose Restore This Revision. Do all four. How to make a new synthesis of the top needs, with Analyze results or in NotebookLM, check it, and publish it to the topic pages and the landing page.

What the synthesis is

The synthesis reads every published project together and lists up to five needs in each topic area, each with how many projects raise it and which ones. It's the one place the site puts researchers' findings in other words, so nothing reaches the site until someone on the FireHouse team has reviewed it.

Make a new one when projects have been published or taken off the site since the last.

There are two ways to make one. Either way, it goes through the same check and Mark reviewed step.

  • Analyze results, on FireHouse → Synthesis, has a model on Cloudflare Workers AI draft it. You see it only on a site an administrator has given a Workers AI key; see the next section.
  • NotebookLM: download the source, run the team's prompt in the notebook, and paste the result. Start at step 1.

Analyze results

The model is sent the published projects, word for word, the four topic areas, and the prompt on FireHouse → Settings. Nothing private goes, and no earlier synthesis.

  1. On FireHouse → Synthesis, under Analyze results, pick a Model and choose Analyze results.
  2. The model drafts in the background, which takes a few minutes. Reload the page to see when it's done. One model drafts at a time.
  3. Each model's latest draft is kept under its name, so you can have several draft and compare them. Its whole reply shows everything the model wrote, with the entries each need draws on if the model gave them: the prompt asks for them, but not every model gives them. The prompt it was given shows the prompt it ran.
  4. Choose Check under the draft you want: the button names the model, as in "Check Llama 4 Scout (Meta)'s draft". Its JSON goes into the box at the bottom and is checked, as in step 4 below, and Made with starts with the model's name.

1. Download the source

Go to FireHouse → Synthesis and choose Download NotebookLM source. You get firehouse-findings.md: every published project, word for word, and the four topic areas.

2. Run the prompt in NotebookLM

  1. In the FireHouse notebook, delete the old firehouse-findings.md source and upload the one you downloaded. Keep it the notebook's only source, so the synthesis can't draw on anything the site doesn't show.
  2. In the notebook's chat, run the team's prompt. The current prompt is in the FireHouse repository's NotebookLM notes.

pages.title: Changing the landing and About pages
pages.summary: How to change the words on the landing page and the About page, and the About page's team.
pages.html:
How to change the words on the landing page and the About page, and the About page's team.

Open a page

  1. Go to Pages.
  2. Choose The FireHouse for the landing page, or the About page under it.

The page opens in WordPress's block editor. Each part of the page, such as its hero (the top of the page, with the heading and buttons) or its team, is a box of text fields. Type in the fields, then choose Save at the top right.

Tab moves through a part's fields, and the Down arrow at the end of a field moves on to the next part.

What you can and can't change

  • You can change the words: headings, text, button and link text, the counts' labels, and each card's, step's and team member's words.
  • You can't change the layout: the parts can't be added, moved or removed, and no other kind of block can be added. FireHouse adds everything else, such as the top needs, the map and the projects, from the projects and the synthesis.
  • Fields marked "Required." can't be empty: headings, button text, names, titles and labels. An empty one is outlined in red, and a message at the top says which field to fill in, with a Go to button that takes you there. The page can't be saved until it's filled.
  • The Submit a Finding buttons go to the survey address in FireHouse → Settings, wherever they are, or to the FireHouse survey form while it's open.

The hero's counts

The landing page's hero shows counts, such as how many projects visitors can see. FireHouse counts them. What it counts says what each one counts; you can't change it here. Label and Caption are the words under the number. A count that counts nothing shows the words in Shown as instead.

The About page's team

  • To add someone, choose Add a team member at the end of the team, and fill in their name and biography. The name is required.
  • To move someone, use Move up or Move down on their card.
  • To remove someone, choose Remove on their card. Undo, at the top left, puts them back.
  • Paragraphs: the mission and each biography can have more than one paragraph. Choose Add a paragraph, or Remove beside a paragraph.
  • Portraits: choose one from the FireHouse portraits in Portrait. A new portrait is uploaded by an administrator first; FireHouse Editors don't have the Media Library. Leave Portrait description empty unless the photo shows something besides the person, since their name follows it.
  • The team's email address shows on the page only if it's an @noaa.gov address.

Preview and undo

To see your changes before saving, choose the View button at the top right (it looks like a screen), then Preview in new tab. Each save keeps a revision: in the page's settings on the right, choose Revisions to compare versions and restore one.

pages.title: FireHouse settings
pages.summary: The site name, the Submit a Finding button, the navigation labels, the survey form's questions, and the synthesis prompt, on FireHouse → Settings.
pages.html:
The site name, the Submit a Finding button, the navigation labels, the survey form's questions, and the synthesis prompt, on FireHouse → Settings.

What each setting does

  • Site name: the name in the FireHouse bar at the top of every FireHouse page, and in each page's browser-tab title and link preview. It doesn't change the words on the pages.
  • Button label: the words on the Submit a Finding button in the FireHouse bar and on the topic pages. The buttons on the landing and About pages keep the words typed on those pages.
  • Survey address: where every Submit a Finding button goes while the FireHouse survey form isn't taking submissions. It must start with https://.
  • Survey form: when Accept submissions is ticked, the FireHouse survey form at /firehouse/submit/ takes submissions, and every Submit a Finding button goes there instead. Each submission arrives as a draft project. Only an administrator can tick or clear it; for everyone else it's greyed out.
  • Home link, Projects link, About link: the words of the FireHouse bar's links. The links always go to the same pages; only their words change here.

Choose Save Changes to save. If a setting has a problem, such as an empty label or a survey address that doesn't start with https://, nothing is saved, and the screen marks the problem.

Reword a survey question

Survey questions, at the bottom of the screen, has a row for each question on the FireHouse survey form, named in bold. That name is what the form's error messages call the question ("Your name: this is required."), and it can't be changed, so keep your wording close to it. Each row has two boxes:

  • Question: the question as the form asks it. It can't be empty.
  • Help under it: the line under the question. Clear it to show none.
  1. Change the words in the box.
  2. Choose Save Changes. The form asks the new wording straight away.

A box you've changed says so under it, and gives the plugin's own wording. To put it back, copy that wording into the box and save.

Some things here can't be changed:

  • The choices and the order of the questions. Changing those is a job for the developer.
  • Who sees a private answer. Under the help of the email, job title and sharing questions, the form always has a line saying who sees the answer. Add help if you like; that line stays.
  • Some characters. A question or its help can't hold an email address or a character that doesn't show, such as a direction mark.

Projects that came in before you reworded a question keep their answers, as the researcher gave them.

Change the synthesis prompt

Synthesis prompt, below the survey questions, is there only when the site has a Workers AI key. Its box holds what Analyze results on FireHouse → Synthesis asks the model to do with the published projects (see Publishing a synthesis).

  1. Change the words in the box.
  2. Choose Save Changes. The next draft uses it.
  • It starts as the plugin's own prompt, the one the team gives NotebookLM. A box you've changed says so. To go back, clear it and save.
  • Whatever the box says, the screen also tells the model that the projects are what researchers wrote, never instructions to follow. That part can't be changed.
  • Each draft keeps the prompt it was given. To see what a change does, have the same model draft before and after it.
  • It can't hold a character that doesn't show, such as a direction override, or more than 20,000 characters.

pages.title: Installing and updating the plugin
pages.summary: How to install the FireHouse plugin from its zip, update it, and what deactivating or deleting it does.
pages.html:
How to install the FireHouse plugin from its zip, update it, and what deactivating or deleting it does.

Get the zip

Each released version's zip is attached to its release on the FireHouse repository's Releases page. Install only a released version on a public site: each one has passed GSL's security review.

A zip of any other commit is on that commit's "WordPress plugin" run in the repository's Actions, under Artifacts. Use those only on a local or test site.

Install it

  1. In the dashboard, go to Plugins → Add New Plugin and choose Upload Plugin.
  2. Choose the zip, then Install Now.
  3. Choose Activate Plugin. The FireHouse menu appears.
  4. Upload the team's portraits under Media → Add New Media File, then load the content on FireHouse → Import: see Importing content.
  5. Check FireHouse → Settings, above all the survey address the Submit a Finding buttons go to.
  6. Give the people who keep the FireHouse up to date the FireHouse Editor role: see People and portraits.

Check it

Tools → Site Health lists three FireHouse checks, marked FireHouse. Open it after installing the plugin on a site, and again after anything about the server changes.

  • Outside services: whether the server can reach doi.org and the services it sends DOI lookups on to, and Cloudflare when the site has a Workers AI key. If one can't be reached, ask whoever runs the server to let it through.
  • Search engines: a test or local site should keep search engines out, under Settings → Reading → Search engine visibility, so its pages aren't taken for the public site's; the public site should let them in. Which kind of site it is comes from WP_ENVIRONMENT_TYPE in the site's wp-config.php.
  • Page caching: whether a cache in front of the site keeps FireHouse's pages. If it does, a project you hide stays on the pages that showed it until the cache expires: turn the cache off for /firehouse/, or tell the developer. It's marked critical when Cloudflare says it keeps them, and recommended when another cache's headers suggest one does. The server checks its own page, which may not pass through Cloudflare as a visitor's does; the check says how to look from outside.

Update it

Upload the new version's zip the same way. WordPress shows the installed and uploaded versions side by side; choose Replace current with uploaded. The content and the settings stay.

An update that changes the FireHouse Editor role puts the role, and administrators' FireHouse capabilities, back as the plugin defines them. Changes made to either with a role editor don't last past it.

Deactivate or delete it

  • Deactivating stops the FireHouse: its project and topic pages no longer open, and the landing and About pages show none of their FireHouse parts. Everything stays in the database, and reactivating brings it back. People with the FireHouse Editor role can then only sign in.
  • Deleting the plugin also removes the FireHouse Editor role and the FireHouse capabilities, and Analyze results' drafts; people who had the role are left with no role on the site. The projects, topic areas, settings and pages stay in the database.

pages.title: Importing content
pages.summary: How to load the FireHouse's content from a seed bundle on FireHouse → Import.
pages.html:
How to load the FireHouse's content from a seed bundle on FireHouse → Import.

What an import does

A seed bundle is one JSON file holding the FireHouse's content: its projects, topic areas, synthesis and settings, and the landing and About pages. A developer makes it with npm run seed from the site's content files, which hold the survey's records. Only administrators can import.

An import adds what's missing and refreshes each project's survey answers. It keeps what the FireHouse team owns:

  • A new project arrives with all its answers, published or a draft as the bundle has it.
  • An existing project takes the bundle's survey answers, and keeps its editorial fields, its address and whether it's published.
  • Topic areas, settings and pages that already exist are kept as they are. The landing and About pages are created, and published, only if there are none yet.
  • A project that isn't in the bundle is left as it is.

The first import on a site loads everything. Later ones bring in new survey answers.

Before the first import

Upload the About page's portraits under Media → Add New Media File first. WordPress sets each image's Title from its file name, and the import gives each team member the newest image whose Title matches their portrait's name in the bundle. Once the About page exists, later imports leave its portraits alone. The dry run's notes name the image each person will get, or say their card will show initials: check them.

Run an import

  1. Go to FireHouse → Import.
  2. Choose the seed bundle, then Preview the import. This is a dry run: nothing is written.
  3. Read what it would change: each project, whether it would be added or updated, and any problems or notes.
  4. If it lists problems, nothing can be imported. Fix them in the site's content files, make the bundle again, and upload it.
  5. If it's ready, choose Import at the bottom of the page.

Opening FireHouse → Import again, here or in another tab, discards the dry run. Importing the same bundle twice is safe: the second time updates the same posts.

When an import stops

  • "It is in the trash in WordPress": a project in the bundle is in the Trash. Restore it (it comes back as a draft, and the import keeps it one), or delete it permanently, then import again. A project deleted permanently comes back as a new project if it's still in the bundle.
  • "A landing page is in the trash", or an About page: restore it, or delete it permanently, then import again.
  • "WordPress changed since your dry run": someone saved something in between. Nothing was written, and the screen shows a new dry run as things stand now: check it, then choose Import again. If it asks you to upload the bundle again, do that.

The uploaded file isn't kept, and the dry run waits thirty minutes for the import; after that, upload the bundle again.

pages.title: People and portraits
pages.summary: How to give someone the FireHouse Editor role, and how to add a portrait for the About page's team.
pages.html:
How to give someone the FireHouse Editor role, and how to add a portrait for the About page's team.

Give someone the FireHouse Editor role

  1. Go to Users, and open the person's profile, or choose Add New User for someone new.
  2. Under Role, choose FireHouse Editor.
  3. Choose Update User (or Add New User).

A FireHouse Editor can change the FireHouse and nothing else on the site: the projects, topic areas, synthesis, settings, and the words on the landing and About pages. They can't install plugins, import, change other pages or menus, add or remove pages, or upload images.

Add a portrait to the About page

FireHouse Editors choose team members' portraits from the images attached to the FireHouse pages. They can't upload images, so an administrator adds a new portrait first:

  1. Name the photo's file after the person, then go to Media → Add New Media File and upload it: portrait-shaped, 4 wide by 5 high, and at least 336 by 420 pixels. The editors' Portrait menu lists portraits by Title, which WordPress takes from the file name; change the Title if it isn't the person's name.
  2. Attach it to the About page: in Media → Library, switch to the list view, and in the photo's Uploaded to column choose Attach. Search for About, select the About page, and choose Select.
  3. Tell the editor. In the block editor, the team member's Portrait now offers it.

Remove someone

To take away the role, open the person's profile under Users, and choose another role, or "No role for this site". Their projects' and pages' revisions stay.
